Methylphenidate (classified under ATC code N06BA04) is a central medication in the Danish healthcare system, recognized as the most common pharmacological treatment for Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) [^src2]. Within the national clinical quality databases, the prescription and coverage of methylphenidate are systematically monitored to evaluate the standard of care provided to patients.

Historically, methylphenidate has been a core component of [[indikator-6|Indikator 6]], a national quality indicator that measures the coverage of pharmacological treatment among children and young people with ADHD enrolled in standardized care pathways [^src1]. Recent reports have highlighted the relative strength of pharmacological treatments like methylphenidate in the Danish ADHD effort, noting significant regional variations, such as particularly strong implementation in North Jutland [^src2]. This medical focus is often contrasted with systemic challenges in non-pharmacological interventions, such as psychoeducation [^src2].

As the national ADHD database has expanded its scope to include adult patients, methylphenidate's role in quality monitoring has grown. It is now explicitly included in the calculation of [[indikator-11|Indikator 11]], a newly introduced quality indicator designed to track pharmacological treatment specifically among adults with ADHD [^src3]. In this adult metric, methylphenidate is monitored alongside five other medication types: dexamphetamine, modafinil, atomoxetine, lisdexamphetamine, and guanfacine [^src3].
